newsitem.title: UK: Client pay structure changes for UK ad agencies.
newsitem.headline: Client pay structure changes for UK ad agencies.

text.p: Companies are increasingly replacing old fixed-commission payments to advertising agencies with new flexible fees and thus forcing agencies to justify the work they do, industry sources said on Thursday.

Traditionally, companies have paid ad agencies a preset commission of around 15 per cent of the client's total advertising expenditure, with the remaining "adspend" mostly covering television airtime or other media space.
But now many clients are paying their ad agencies with a mixture of the old preset commissions and new flexible fees and "top-up" payments if a campaign is considered successful.
"There has been a gradual shift away from commission to a fee basis," Paul Simons, chief executive of Simons Palmer Denton Clemmow, which is in the process of merging with TBWA ad agency, said.
"In 1986 probably 98 per cent of all agency remuneration was commission-based. Now it is significantly less," he told Reuters.

A recent survey by specialist accountancy firm, Willott Kingston Smith showd that last year preset commission accounted for about 43 percent of total ad agency income in Britain, while new flexible fees accounted for another 41 percent.
Another way in which clients are forcing ad agencies to justify their work is a growing trend towards performance-related pay.

The study showed "payment by results" accounted for less than two percent of ad agency income in 1996. But a surprising 41 percent of agencies surveyed were receiving some kind of incentive payment from clients and industry sources say the trend is expected to grow.
Clients that stick to the old commission system tend to be large spenders across global consumer-product markets.

"Clients are looking for value for money and agencies are looking for an appropriate margin for the job," says Nick Phillips, director general of Britain's Institute of Practitioners in Advertising (IPA).
Clients such as Procter & Gamble and Unilever tend to stick with commission-based payment because it is the most appropriate for their business," he told Reuters.
A growing number of agencies welcome the shift away from commission-based payments.

Stephen Maher, managing director of London agency MBA said, "If payment is based on fees then it is like being a consultant. The payment is related more to the work's value then to the client's absolute spend."
But ad agencies can lose out if they are paid according to the time spent on a campaign -- and they come up with good advertising ideas fast.
One famous case was the work done by Bartle Bogle Hegarty for its client, Levi jeans.

Its "laundrette" ad starring a hunky male model who peels off his jeans in a laundrette to the accompaniment of Marvin Gaye's track, "I heard it through the grapevine", took the ad agency "creatives" involved less than an hour to develop.
It started some of the most talked about ads of the 1980s and 1990s and made Levi's a fashion icon in Britain.

Another problem for ad agencies with payment by results is that clients are using a growing mix of advertising, direct mail, public relations and sponsorship, which makes it difficult to assess the success of an ad campaign.
Ben Langdon, managing director of McCann-Erickson in Britain is pessimistic about payment by results.
"Future advertising agency remuneration systems will be determined by the future structure of agencies," he told Reuters.

"If agencies move to a lower fixed-overhead base with higher use of freelancers, it would be easier to imagine a payment system more linked towards success-based incentives and ad hoc fees for project work," he said.

"But many clients still feel uneasy about the use of freelancers for reasons of confidentiality, or through fear of a lack of commitment, and until this and other issues are resolved, I fear no real progress will be made," he said.
